Title: The new hardware trigger processor at NA62 experiment: Status of the System and First Results
Text:
The new hardware trigger processor at NA62 experiment:
Status of the System and First Results

Frezza13,∗, Francesca Lo Cicero13, Alessandro Lonardo13, Michele Martinelli1, Pierpaolo

Abstract. The NA62 experiment is designed to study rare and ultra-rare kaon
decays using a decay-in-flight technique. The Trigger and Data Acquisition
(TDAQ) system of NA62 is multi-level, making it critically dependent on the
performance of the inter-level network. To manage the huge amount of data
produced by the detectors, three levels of triggers are employed. The first level
L0TP, implemented using an FPGA device, has been in operation since the start
of data taking in 2016. In order to increase the efficiency of the system and
implement additional algorithms, an upgraded system (L0TP+) was developed
starting in 2018. This upgrade avails itself of a high-end FPGA available on
the market, offering more computing power, larger local memory and higher
transmission bandwidth. We have planned tests for a new trigger algorithm that
implements quadrant-based logic for the veto systems. This new approach is
expected to improve the main trigger efficiency by several percent. Extensive
tests were conducted using a parasitic setup that included a set of Network TAPs
and a commodity server, allowing for proficient comparison of trigger decisions
on an event-by-event basis. The experience gained from this parasitic mode op-
eration can be leveraged for the next data-taking period as a development setup
to implement additional features, thereby accelerating the TDAQ upgrade. Af-
ter the testing period, the new system has been adopted as the online processor
since 2023. Preliminary results on the efficiency of the new system will be
reported. Integration with the new AI-based FPGA-RICH system, which per-
forms online partial particle identification, will also be discussed.
1 Introduction
NA62 is a kaon physics experiment located at CERN North Area which aims to detect ultra-
rare decays of K mesons from a 75 GeV/c positively charged hadron beam. The signals of
interest are extremely rare, necessitating a high-intensity beam paired with multi-level trigger
selectivity.

The lowest level of the NA62 trigger – Level Zero (L0) – is tasked with generating trigger
decisions based on minimal information (referred to as trigger primitives) received from a
subset of detectors, within a latency of less than one millisecond. Our work focuses on up-
grading the hardware of the L0 trigger processor (L0TP, based on Altera Stratix IV), imple-
menting it on a Xilinx VCU118 FPGA board (L0TP+), in order to increase the performance,
fix some inconsistencies and to add new features such as Neural Network-based particle iden-
tification and new trigger algorithms. This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 details
the NA62 experiment with its DAQ system; Section 3 and Section 4 describe the architecture
of L0TP+ and its integration into the NA62 DAQ system; Section 5 discusses the L0TP+
results; and Section 6 introduces the new features of L0TP+.
2 The NA62 experiment
Figure 1. NA62 Experiment layout.
The NA62 experiment is a fixed-target experiment especially designed to measure the
branching ratio of the ultra-rare K+ →π+νν decay [2]. The experiment utilizes a 400 GeV/c
proton beam extracted from the Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS) at CERN. Such a high-
energy proton beam directed onto a beryllium target results in the generation of a 75 GeV/c
secondary hadron beam. This secondary beam is composed of approximately 70% π+, 24%
protons, and 6% K+. These latter are identified using the KTAG, a threshold Cherenkov
detector. The momentum of all particles within the secondary beam is measured with high
precision by the GTK, a silicon pixel beam tracker. These particles then travel through the
experiment’s fiducial decay volume, where the STRAW spectrometer and two scintillator
hodoscopes (CHOD and NA48-CHOD) reconstruct the decays of kaons by measuring the
momentum of the charged decay products. For particle identification purposes, the experi-
ment employs a series of detectors: the Ring Imaging Cherenkov (RICH) Detector, the liquid
krypton (LKr) calorimeter and a muon veto system. Furthermore, to efficiently veto photons
that fall outside the acceptance of the LKr, additional photon detection systems are incorpo-
rated, namely the large- angle (LAV) and small-angle (IRC and SAC) photon detectors. A
schematic representation of the NA62 detector is shown in Figure 1. A detailed description
of the experimental apparatus can be found in [3]. The experiment’s design, incorporating
multiple trigger lines [4], allows for the study of not only the K+ →π+νν decay, but also a
variety of other K+ decay modes.

2.1 Trigger and Data Acquisition system
To manage the high particle flux needed by the NA62 experiment, a sophisticated and unified
Trigger and Data Acquisition (TDAQ) system is essential, for minimizing dead time and
ensuring reliable data collection in a cost-effective manner. This system employs Time-to-
Digital Converters (TDCs) for the readout of most detectors, with exceptions of the LKr
calorimeter, of the MUV1 and MUV2 muon detectors which utilize 14-bit Flash Analog-to-
Digital Converters (FADCs) and the IRC and SAC detectors which use both. Custom-made
TEL62 boards are mainly used for TDC readout and trigger information processing while
specialized TDC boards are implemented for the GTK and STRAW detectors. The NA62
trigger system is arranged as two levels that throttle the ∼10 MHz data rate down to about
100 kHz:
– the L0 Trigger Processor [5], implemented using an FPGA programmable logic device;
– the L1 trigger implemented in software on a computer farm.
L0TP parses primitives (Ethernet UDP packets) from CHODs, MUV3, RICH, LKr and LAV
detectors (Fig. 2) to generate a low-level trigger that initiates data readout. Afterwards, a
software-based trigger (L1) further refines the data selection, using reconstruction algorithms
similar to those of offline analysis. Exploiting the information from the KTAG, LAV and
STRAW detectors, L1 reduces the data volume before storage of an additional factor ∼20.

Figure 3. Architecture of L0TP+. Primitives, sent by detectors packed in MTP, are time-aligned and
stored in RAM blocks. The MMU block, using the address specified by primitives from the reference
detector (stored in the REF FIFO), synchronizes the primitives read from the RAMs, and sends them
to the trigger logic. The output trigger is sent to all the NA62 detectors while the trigger information,
packed into MEPs, is dispatched to the NA62 PC-FARM.
calorimeters or the hit-multiplicity and topology in the hodoscope) and their time of occur-
rence, via dedicated Ethernet links to L0TP+. Several primitives can be packed together into
Multi-Trigger Packets (MTP), to optimize data transmission.
After compensating the eventual offset between received Ethernet packets using FIFOs
[5], primitives are stored into a RAM (one for each detector), using the timing information –
a timestamp – to generate the appropriate memory address, ensuring their correct alignment
in time.
During the writing process, a specific detector is assumed as reference source (usually the
RICH due to its intrinsic timing precision): the memory addresses of the reference detector
primitives are stored into a dedicated FIFO (REF FIFO).
All RAMs are read from the MMU (Memory management unit) using the memory ad-
dresses specified in the REF FIFO, ensuring that all subsystems are in sync with respect to the
reference detector. The read primitives are collected into a bit vector called current_state and
transmitted to the trigger logic. Each of these bits depends on the type of the event measured
by the detector.
During the initialization of L0TP+ a set of registers are filled and used to form various
masks. Current_state is then bit-wise compared to the masks and a trigger is issued if at least
one of mask criteria is satisfied. The output trigger is sent to all the NA62 detectors, while
the trigger information is dispatched to the NA62 PC-Farm, packed into Multi-Event-Packets
(MEPs). Since the reference detector is present by construction in all the trigger masks, it
is impossible to measure trigger efficiency without additional information. To address this
issue, a control detector able to generate triggers was added. This solution allows creating
two different samples of events, one collected by the reference detector and the other by the
control one. Although these two samples are uncorrelated streams of data in the FPGA, they
are correlated from the point of view of the physics. This correlation allows to measure the
efficiency of each trigger mask.
Together with the primitives, the L0TP+ handles asynchronous choke signals sent from
detectors, suspending trigger generation and preventing memory overflow. In addition, in

L0TP+ an auto-choke mechanism is implemented to avoid the overflow of output memory
buffer in case of a peak in the number of primitives received. Thanks to the large amount
of BRAM of the VCU118 board, the number of auto-choke invocations during the Run has
significantly decreased compared to that of the previous version of the Level 0 trigger (L0TP).
In order to let the Run Control [1] configure and check the status of L0TP+, a Micro-
controller connected to the the DIM (Distributed Information Management) server is used as
interface.
A common coherent clock – with a frequency of approximately 40 MHz and generated
centrally by a single free-running high-stability oscillator – is distributed optically to all sys-
tems through the Timing, Trigger and Control (TTC) system [7].
4 L0TP+ integration and validation
In order to validate the new Trigger Processor during the 2023 Run, a dedicated setup was
built at the experiment. By means of a Network TAP (Test Access Point) we are able to
duplicate the primitives coming from the detectors and send them to either the L0TP and
L0TP+ systems as shown in Fig. 4. As described in 3, once L0TP produces the Trigger,
all information is stored in packets called MEPs which are forwarded to the PC-Farm; by
means of a second Network TAP these packets are also duplicated and sent to a dedicated
server where the information of the Trigger produced by L0TP+ is collected. We developed
a dedicated UDP packet sniffer able to read all information produced by the two systems and
compare them. After this validation process, L0TP+ has become the Trigger Processor for
the experiment starting from the first leg of 2023 data taking.
The configuration used to validate the system – the one with a parasitic L0TP+ – was
maintained in order to develop new features and easily validate them.

5 L0TP+ results
After the validation period, it is since 2023 that L0TP+ has been enrolled in the NA62 exper-
iment as the upgrade of the Level zero Trigger.
The system is very stable and a preliminary measurement of efficiency was performed
using data processed after some months of the 2023 Run. In Fig. 6 is represented the number
of Kaons decays to two pions per 4.8 s Burst using the old trigger processor (L0TP in red) and
the new one (L0TP+ in green). The line in blue represents the efficiency of an early version
of the L0TP+ firmware, before a bug was fixed.

6 L0TP+ new capabilities
The new device the L0TP+ IP is deployed on has many high-speed ports available (10 SFP+
@25Gbps, two QSFP and two FireFly ports up to @100Gbps) and a large percentage of

FPGA resources left unused (∼70% of BRAM, 80% of LUTs and 99% of DSPs); this pro-
vides a wide headroom to add new functionalities to the core design.
As a first step, a 32-bit MicroBlaze Soft-Core microcontroller with support for both bare-
metal and Petalinux software environments has been integrated to enhance the configuration
and debugging capabilities.
The integration of a PCI-Express interface and a streaming processing module is planned
for future releases. An additional analysis has been performed to evaluate the integration of
a single MUV quadrant-based trigger to reduce the current over veto probability.
6.1 Stream processing module
The increasing interest in leveraging FPGAs for computational acceleration is also focusing
attention toward High-Level Synthesis (HLS) as a means to simplify application development
on FPGAs.
HLS enables the employ of programmable logic directly converting C/C++ functions
into logic modules, therefore bypassing the effort of translating these functions to a tradi-
tional hardware description language like Verilog or VHDL. Waiting for the results of one
operation before initiating the next is often inefficient. By translating synthesized functions
into logic elements, HLS enables the use of multiple pipelining stages, allowing the logic
to process different data sets simultaneously through overlapping operations. With the goal
of handling primitives or even raw data streams from additional sub-detectors and enhanc-
ing trigger efficiency, we added a reconfigurable module in the design, the stream processing
module, to take advantage of the new capabilities offered by L0TP+ in conjunction with HLS.
We foresee the integration of one such module in the form of a Neural Network-based
system called FPGA-RICH [6] that uses as an input the RICH detector raw hit data stream at
L0 and produces physics-based primitives (i.e. the number of charged particles in the physics
event).
6.2 New trigger algorithm
The Muon Veto detector is used in most of the trigger masks to reduce the rate from muon
halo and dominant K to muon neutrino decay. The presence of the MUV system in the trigger
causes a random veto probability of ∼8-10% on genuine events in most of the L0 Trigger
Masks. In the current implementation the presence of events in the MUV causes rejection of
the event independently from which part of the new CHOD system is firing (see Fig. 7).
In order to reduce the random veto probability, the geometrical information (quadrant)
provided by the new CHOD and MUV primitives can be used. To realize the quadrant-based
logic, a new feature in the Trigger algorithm is needed: the capability to perform a ’Logic
OR’ condition in addition to the ’Logic AND’ condition in the trigger logic module of the
firmware.
7 Conclusion
This paper presents the upgrade of the L0 Trigger Processor (L0TP+) for the NA62 exper-
iment. It describes the architecture of the design implemented on the VCU118 board, its
integration in the experiment and its validation. Preliminary results show significant improve-
ments in terms of performance, reliability and efficiency compared to the previous iteration
of the trigger processor. The uptick in available resources in modern FPGAs also allows
implementing new functionalities such as Neural Network-based feature recognition systems
for particle identification (like FPGA-RICH [6]) and enhanced trigger algorithms.

Abstract: The NA62 experiment is designed to study rare and ultra-rare kaon decays using a decay-in-flight technique. The Trigger and Data Acquisition (TDAQ) system of NA62 is multi-level, making it critically dependent on the performance of the inter-level network. To manage the huge amount of data produced by the detectors, three levels of triggers are employed. The first level L0TP, implemented using an FPGA device, has been in operation since the start of data taking in 2016. In order to increase the efficiency of the system and implement additional algorithms, an upgraded system (L0TP+) was developed starting in 2018. This upgrade avails itself of a high-end FPGA available on the market, offering more computing power, larger local memory and higher transmission bandwidth. We have planned tests for a new trigger algorithm that implements quadrant-based logic for the veto systems. This new approach is expected to improve the main trigger efficiency by several percent. Extensive tests were conducted using a parasitic setup that included a set of Network TAPs and a commodity server, allowing for proficient comparison of trigger decisions on an event-by-event basis. The experience gained from this parasitic mode op- eration can be leveraged for the next data-taking period as a development setup to implement additional features, thereby accelerating the TDAQ upgrade. Af- ter the testing period, the new system has been adopted as the online processor since 2023. Preliminary results on the efficiency of the new system will be reported. Integration with the new AI-based FPGA-RICH system, which per- forms online partial particle identification, will also be discussed.
